entry.title: What happens inside a 3D click
entry.content:
Junhan Kong1, Jacqui Fashimpaur2, Michael J. Proulx2, Hemant Bhaskar Surale2, Jacob O. Wobbrock1, Amy Karlson2
1University of Washington  ·  2Reality Labs Research, Meta
Conference paper · ICMI '26: International Conference on Multimodal Interaction, Napoli, Italy
PDF ACM DL Publication BibTeX
The five techniques we tested: a participant's posture while pointing (top), the target before selection (middle), and the target during selection (bottom). Figure from the paper.

Quick facts

A VR selection is not a single instant. Between press and release, which took about 0.17 seconds on average in our study, the ray, eyes, head, and hand all keep moving. Overall, our work contributes:

  1. Eight measures that characterize pointer movement, gaze, head, and hand movement, and the alignment between gaze and pointer during a selection.
  2. A validation study with 36 participants, five 3D pointing techniques, and 13,885 trials, showing that the measures track accuracy, throughput, task load, exertion, and user experience.
  3. Design implications for 3D pointing: tolerate less stable pointing, prioritize speed and low latency, and design for coordination across modalities.

Abstract

Measures of target selection in virtual reality (VR) have focused mainly on overall performance, such as speed and accuracy. However, a selection is not atomic: numerous things happen during the short “click” when a target is selected. In this work, we formalize a set of measures that provide insight into what happens during this process. The measures characterize the pointer movement, user behaviors (gaze, head, hand and finger), and coordination between modalities. To validate the measures, we collected pointing data from 36 participants using five different 3D pointing techniques. Our results show that these measures effectively characterize pointing performance, task load, perceived exertion, ease of use/learning, comfort, and sense of agency. We found that tolerating less “stable” pointing and considering alignment between modalities both improve pointing performance. Our findings suggest that 3D pointing should prioritize speed, allow for more movements during selection, and consider coordination of different modalities.

The idea: look inside the click

When we compare pointing techniques in VR, we usually report speed and accuracy, which treat a selection as a single instant. Instead, we recorded every sensor sample between selection start and selection end (about 12 samples per click) and computed measures over that window.

The timeline shows what each modality does during one selection, with the measure we compute from it. The task-plane view shows the alignment measures, which compare where the pointer and the eyes land.

We started from 31 candidate measures and kept the eight that correlated with performance and user ratings and were easiest to interpret. They fall into three groups:

  • Pointer: how much the ray direction jitters (pointer direction variability) and how far the cursor wanders on the target plane (hit point variability).
  • Single modality: how far the eyes and head turn (gaze and head direction range), how far the palm moves (palm position drift), and how much the index fingertip moves (index fingertip variability).
  • Alignment: how far apart the pointer and gaze land on average (mean alignment distance), and where the pointer was at the moment it agreed most with gaze (alignment-adjusted endpoint).

The measures only need the sensor samples from inside the click, so they are cheap enough to compute at runtime.

Experiment

Techniques. We chose five techniques that cover different pointing modalities (controller, gaze, hand, finger) and selection triggers (button, pinch, thumb tap), from widely used controllers to a novel wearable.

The five techniques. Controller: point and click with the controller. Gaze-Contr: look, then press the controller button. Gaze-Pinch: look, then pinch. Handray: a ray from the palm, select by pinching. Ring: a ray from a ring on the index finger (ElectroRing), select with a thumb tap. Figure from the paper.

Apparatus. A Unity testbed on a Meta Quest Pro. Gaze, head, and controller were recorded at 72 Hz and hand tracking at 60 Hz. The ring prototype (ElectroRing) combines a 9-axis IMU with electrodes that detect the thumb tap.

Task. Gray spherical targets appeared one at a time at random positions within ±35° of the center of view, 2 m away, in two sizes (5° and 10°). Each technique and size combination had 5 practice and 40 test trials.

Participants. 36 people (14 women, 22 men, mean age 36.1), 35 of them right-handed. After removing outliers, we kept 13,885 valid trials (98.4%).

Measures. Hit or miss for every trial, plus ratings after each block: NASA-TLX task load, Borg CR-10 perceived exertion, and ease of use, ease of learning, comfort, and sense of agency.

What do we learn?

1. Steadier clicks are more accurate

Across individual trials, the less the ray moved during the click, the more often it hit the target.

(a) Accuracy by technique and target size. (b) Blocks with more pointer movement during the click had lower accuracy. Figure from the paper.

2. But techniques that let you hold still were slower and more tiring

Ranked by throughput, which combines speed and accuracy, the order was Controller (2.49 bits/s), Gaze-Contr (2.23), Gaze-Pinch (1.94), Ring (1.75), and Handray (1.34). Handray had the least pointer movement during the click and the highest physical demand. Controller had the most movement and the lowest physical demand.

Pointer direction variability (left) and physical demand (right) move in opposite directions across techniques. Figure from the paper.

The same pattern held for task load, perceived exertion, ease of use, comfort, and sense of agency: less movement during the click went with worse ratings. Holding a ray perfectly still in mid-air takes effort in a way that resting a finger on a touchscreen does not, so speed mattered more than accuracy for overall performance.

3. Eyes and hands work as a team

For the three techniques that don’t point with gaze (Controller, Handray, Ring), we scored each click using the alignment-adjusted endpoint instead of the release position. The hit rate went from 91.8% to 93.6%: 196 misses became hits and 52 hits became misses. We also found correlations across modalities. For example, gaze range was linked to hand and finger exertion, and mean alignment distance was linked to task load.

Design implications

  1. Tolerate less stable pointing. Don’t make users hold a ray perfectly still to select.
  2. Prioritize movement speed over pointing accuracy.
  3. Prioritize low latency over sensing accuracy. Participants called Handray “laggy” and felt more in control when the pointer “actually followed the movement”.
  4. Design for coordination. Gaze, head, and hands move together during a click, and using that alignment can rescue near misses.

Limitations

We tested spherical targets at a fixed 2 m distance on a vertical plane, in fully virtual environments only, using the Quest Pro’s default eye and hand tracking. Handray was sampled at 60 Hz versus 72 Hz for the others, which may account for some of its differences. Extending the measures to AR, other target layouts, and real-world tasks is future work.

entry.title: Does explaining an AI moderator make it easier to trust?

link.title: Does explaining an AI moderator make it easier to trust?

entry.content:
Kamalakkannan Ravi1, Hemant Surale2, Jiann-Shiun Yuan1
1University of Central Florida  ·  2University of Waterloo
Workshop paper · WEB&GRAPH 2026: Workshop on Web & Graphs, Responsible Intelligence, and Social Media at WSDM 2026, Boise, ID, USA
🏆 Best Paper Award
PDF ACM DL Publication BibTeX
The Total Freedom Interface (TFI), our moderation interface, showing the LIME explanation (XAI Method 2) for one message: the predicted label, the score for each class, each word's contribution, and the influential words highlighted in the text. Figure from the paper.

Quick facts

A threat classifier can be accurate and still hard to act on if moderators cannot see why it chose a label. We put a classifier’s prediction next to three kinds of explanations and measured how much 31 people trusted it, how clear they found it, and how long they took. Led by Kamalakkannan Ravi (University of Central Florida). Overall, our work contributes:

  1. An evaluation framework for trust and explainability, built into a live moderation interface that places three complementary explanation views next to the model’s prediction and maps them to measured trust, usability, and perceived effectiveness.
  2. A within-subjects user study (n=31) of how explanation clarity, response time, and format affect trust, usability, and moderation behavior.
  3. Statistical evidence linking explanation clarity to trust, and trust to perceived moderation effectiveness.
  4. Design guidelines: prioritize low cognitive load visualizations, keep response times fast enough for real-time decisions, and explore hybrid explanation formats.

Abstract

As online social platforms face increasing challenges in moderating nuanced threats across web communities, trust in automated moderation systems is critical. TRuST-M examines this problem in web and social-network environments, where moderation occurs under time pressure and public scrutiny. Large language models (LLMs) achieve strong classification performance but remain difficult to interpret, reducing user confidence and accountability in real-world workflows. This work introduces TRuST-M, a human-centered evaluation framework that studies how explanation methods influence trust, understanding, and perceived effectiveness in LLM-based threat moderation. The framework integrates a RoBERTa model pretrained on 1M Telegram posts and fine-tuned on 15,063 labeled messages across three classes (No Threat, Judicial Threat, Non-Judicial Threat), achieving 95.8% accuracy, weighted F1 of 0.96, and Cohen’s kappa of 0.94 on a held-out set. A within-subjects study (n=31) evaluated six messages of varying complexity with predictions and three explanation methods: Integrated Gradients, LIME, and attention visualization. LIME was preferred by 58% of participants for its intuitive word-level highlights, though longer response times were noted, while attention visualizations were rated least helpful due to unclear token emphasis. Statistical analysis revealed positive correlations between explanation clarity, user trust, and confidence in moderation decisions. We frame TRuST-M as an interpretable decision-support system for human-in-the-loop moderation, emphasizing calibrated trust and moderator comprehension rather than model replacement. The findings show that explanation clarity and response time meaningfully shape trust and decision confidence in AI-assisted moderation, advancing transparent, usable, and trustworthy moderation tools for the social web.

The idea: one verdict, three explanations

TRuST-M stands for Threat Reasoning and User Study of Trust in Moderation. The goal is to support a human moderator, not replace one. A participant picks a message, the classifier labels it, and three explanation methods each show which words drove the label. We then asked whether people trusted the label, whether the explanations were clear, and whether the tool would help them moderate.

One message goes through the classifier, which scores each class, and then through three explanation methods. The example message and the LIME word weights come from the interface screenshot in the paper; the Method 1 and Method 3 sketches are schematic. The second panel shows the ratings we collected and how strongly they correlated.

The classifier uses a three-class taxonomy that separates lawful punitive speech from calls for violence:

  • No Threat: strongly worded but non-harmful expressions (“Live free or die”).
  • Judicial Threat: advocacy for legal or punitive action (“Lock her up”).
  • Non-Judicial Threat: direct or implied calls for unlawful violence (“It’s time to start a civil war”). Mixed cases default to this class.

System

Data. We collected replies from far-left and far-right Telegram channels (far-right content dominated because those channels post more). Of 2.3M replies, 15,076 were annotated with criminology-informed guidelines, and 15,063 remained after resolving borderline cases. We split them into training (10,554), development (2,248), and test (2,261) sets.

Model. We first pretrained RoBERTa on 1M unlabeled Telegram replies (12,260 steps, about 137 hours) and then fine-tuned it on the labeled set for 100 epochs (about 168 hours). On the held-out test set it reached 95.8% accuracy, a weighted F1 of 0.96, and a Cohen’s kappa of 0.94.

Interface. The Total Freedom Interface is a web app built with Streamlit. A participant selects a message, presses Predict, sees a color-coded label with class probabilities, and then opens each explanation method. Each method uses its own view (heatmaps, bar charts, or token highlighting). The interface logs the time from Start Timer to End Timer for each message.

Study

Task. Each participant reviewed six Telegram replies from the test set, two per class: one “easy” (explicit threat markers, unanimous annotator agreement) and one “hard” (implicit, sarcastic, or context-dependent language). For every message they viewed the prediction and examined all three explanation methods. The message order was fixed.

Participants. 31 people (15 female, 16 male) aged 18 to 44. Thirteen had prior moderation experience, including two professional moderators, and 81.2% had never used an explainable AI tool.

Procedure. About 30 minutes: an onboarding demo with a neutral example and a content warning (5 minutes), the six messages (10 to 15 minutes), and a survey with open-ended feedback (10 minutes).

Measures. Interaction time per message; 1 to 5 ratings of trust in the model, perceived explainability, and moderation effectiveness; a 19-item usability assessment; and open-ended comments. After cleaning (fewer than 4% of trials dropped), the data covered 558 explanation interactions and 186 timed tasks.

Mean ratings across all explanation methods: usability 4.27, trust 4.25, explainability 4.16, and confidence in moderation decisions 3.99 (error bars show standard deviation). Figure from the paper.

What do we learn?

1. Clearer explanations went with more trust

Participants who found the explanations clearer also trusted the model more (Spearman ρ = 0.493, p = 0.005). Trust in turn correlated with perceived moderation effectiveness (ρ = 0.62, p < 0.01), and so did explainability (ρ = 0.66, p < 0.01). So even with a model that is 95.8% accurate, trust went hand in hand with understanding its output.

Spearman correlations among the four ratings. Figure from the paper.

Usability got the highest ratings (mean 4.27, SD 0.56) but correlated less with trust (ρ = 0.38, p < 0.05) than clarity did. Comments said the hard part was interpreting the explanations, not using the controls. Usability helps, but it is not enough for trust. Education level was linked to usability satisfaction: 83% of PhD holders rated the system “Excellent” or “Best Imaginable”, while 50% of Bachelor’s degree holders rated it “Good” or “Fair” (χ²(6, N=31) = 20.99, p < 0.05). We found no significant effects of gender, age, or prior AI/ML experience.

2. LIME was the favorite, attention the least helpful

18 of 31 participants (58%) preferred Method 2 (LIME) for its color-coded highlights and ranked word importance. P23: “Method 2 was the most helpful, as it clearly separated the words that were important for the label given.” The catch was speed. P10: “Faster XAI method 2 implementation would help [for a] real-world use case.”

Method 3 (attention) drew the most criticism for confusing scores and emphasis on uninformative tokens. P19 noted that it “was often giving higher attention to special tokens like inverted commas”. Many participants were also confused when different methods highlighted different words for the same message, and a few suggested combining methods. P13 thought combining Methods 2 and 3 “would be easier for general people to interpret”.

3. Messages that looked severe got a second look

Hard messages usually took longer: the easy No Threat message took 112.5 s on average and its hard counterpart 160.3 s. The exception was the judicial threat: the easy one took the longest of all six (183.2 s), longer than the hard one (147.6 s). When content looks clearly severe, people may spend extra time checking the AI’s output before accepting it.

Mean interaction time for each of the six messages, which includes reviewing the prediction and all three explanations. Figure from the paper.

Design implications

  1. Prioritize simple, local visualizations. Highlight the words that matter and avoid visual clutter.
  2. Treat latency as a first-class design constraint. The preferred method (LIME) was also slow to respond, and slow explanations lose value in fast-paced moderation.
  3. Adopt hybrid explanation strategies. Combine word-level highlights with lightweight visual overviews.
  4. Match explanation depth to risk. Offer a quick review mode for routine items and a deep review mode for critical or ambiguous ones.

Limitations

The study had 31 participants and only two professional moderators, so the results may not hold for expert teams or large-scale operations. Message order and the mapping of method labels were fixed, which may have introduced order and framing effects. It was a single-session lab study, and LIME’s latency was noted by participants but not quantified. The training data came mostly from far-right channels, which may skew predictions and increase false positives for some ideological groups. Future work includes cohorts of more than 50 moderators across platforms, randomized designs, and field deployments.

entry.title: From screen to audio and back while walking

link.title: From screen to audio and back while walking

entry.content:
Ruei-Che Chang1, Tovi Grossman2, Carine Rognon1, Michael Glueck1, Christopher Collins1, Amy Karlson1, Hemant Bhaskar Surale1
1Reality Labs Research, Meta  ·  2University of Toronto
Conference paper · UIST '25: ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology, Busan, Republic of Korea
PDF ACM DL Publication BibTeX
A Viago scenario. (a) While waiting for an order, the user taps the orange button and gets a visual and audio preview of what will be available by ear. (b) Walking to pick up the order, they navigate by touch gestures and audio feedback; an important action such as submit is held for visual confirmation. (c) Back at the seat, a visual and audio review refreshes what they heard and did, and the held action is restored so they can finish it visually. Figure from the paper.

Quick facts

Looking down at a phone while walking splits your attention between the screen and the street. Viago lets you start browsing by looking, keep going by listening with the phone at your side, and pick up where you left off when you look again. The work was led by Ruei-Che Chang (University of Michigan) during a research internship at Reality Labs Research, Meta. Overall, our work contributes:

  1. Design insights and guidelines from a design probe study with ten users, for reducing cognitive load and supporting continuity and quick resumption when switching between visual and audio modalities on the go.
  2. Viago, a smartphone background service that provides multimodal feedback and interaction techniques for seamless transitions between visual and audio modalities.
  3. A preliminary evaluation with thirteen mobile users that shows the limitations, feasibility, and promise of Viago.
  4. Broader design implications for intelligent, seamless modality switching in on-the-go contexts.

Abstract

As mobile phone use while walking becomes increasingly prevalent, users often divide their visual attention between their surroundings and phone displays, raising concerns around safety and interaction efficiency. Alternative input and output modalities (such as eyes-free touch gestures and audio feedback) offer a promising avenue for reducing visual demands in these contexts. However, the design of seamless transitions between visual and audio modalities for mobile interaction on the go remains underexplored. To fill this gap, we conducted a design probe study with ten participants, simulating screen reader-like experiences across diverse applications to identify five key design insights and three design guidelines. Informed by these insights, we developed Viago, a background service that facilitates fluid transitions between visual and audio modalities for mobile task management while walking. A subsequent evaluation with thirteen participants demonstrated that Viago effectively supports on-the-go interactions by enabling users to interleave modalities as needed. We conclude by discussing the broader implications of visual-audio modality transitions and their potential to enhance mobile interactions in everyday, dynamic environments.

The idea: hand the feed from eyes to ears, and back

Screen readers already let blind and low-vision people use a phone through touch gestures and audio. Viago borrows that model for anyone on the move, and focuses on the two hand-offs that a screen reader does not handle: visual to audio (V2A) before you start walking, and audio to visual (A2V) when you look at the screen again.

The first diagram follows one trip through Viago's three modes, with the scenario from the paper underneath. The second shows how audio mode turns a feed into a two-level list you can skim by headline and open on demand.

Two design choices make this work. First, what you hear in audio mode is set up while you can still see: the same headline you hear while looking is where audio mode starts, and the orange outlines tell you exactly which elements you will be able to reach by ear. Second, high-visibility actions that you take by ear, such as sharing or reposting, are not sent right away. They wait until you look at the screen and confirm them.

System

We first ran a design probe study (see Studies below) and turned its five insights into three guidelines, one for each stage: the visual-to-audio transition, consuming content on the go, and the audio-to-visual transition. Viago implements one set of techniques per stage.

Viago's modes and their input and feedback. (a) V2A mode starts with the orange button and adds enhanced visual and audio feedback. (b) Audio mode starts when the phone is lowered and offers hierarchical audio navigation, plus high-contrast visuals for quick glances. (c) A2V mode starts when the user looks at the phone again and highlights what they did in audio mode. Figure from the paper.

V2A mode. Tapping the orange button outlines the current post in orange (it will be read first) and then outlines the elements that will be available in audio mode: author name, timestamp, post content, images, and the buttons the user cares about. Buttons are picked semi-automatically: an element clicked 3 times within 1 minute is added, and a single tap adds or dismisses any element. In V2A mode, each new post the user scrolls to is announced with an audio headline (author name and timestamp), and tapping a button gives spatial feedback such as “Like button clicked” from the left. The first thing heard in audio mode is therefore already familiar.

Audio mode. It starts when Viago detects that the user has looked away: no face in the front camera and the phone held down at their side. Gestures work anywhere on the screen: swipe up or down for the next or previous post, swipe left or right between elements in a post, single tap to enter or exit a post, and double tap to select. Only the elements chosen in V2A mode are in the list. Spatial audio places sounds where the element sits on screen (the author’s name on the left, buttons on the right), text is read in a female voice and image descriptions in a male voice, and vibrations confirm each gesture. For quick glances, the screen dims everything except the focused element. Actions with high visibility, such as sharing or reposting, are cached.

A2V mode. When the user looks again, a blue button jumps to the first post they heard in audio mode, and tapping it again returns to the latest one. Posts they heard and elements they used are outlined in blue, the same audio headlines play again, and cached actions pop up so they can be confirmed and finished visually.

Viago runs as an Android application on a Pixel 7 Pro and uses Android’s built-in text-to-speech. It reads the screen through Android’s Accessibility Service and flattens the interface into a list for gesture navigation, an approach reused from the design probe.

Studies

We ran two studies: a design probe to learn what people need when switching modalities on the go, and a first-use evaluation of Viago.

Study 1: design probe

Probe. A screen reader-like audio mode that worked on participants’ own apps, with automatic switching between visual and audio modes based on face detection and phone orientation.

Task. In a simulated coffee shop, participants used their phone visually while seated (30 seconds), walked to pick up an order in audio mode (60 seconds), and returned to their seat to continue visually (30 seconds). Chimes marked the transitions. They repeated this for three of their own apps and then brainstormed improvements.

Participants. Ten mobile users (6 male, 4 female) who used apps such as Facebook, LinkedIn, Instagram, Spotify, and Gmail.

What we found. Five insights. People kept a mental picture of the screen layout and wanted anchors to it. Hearing everything on screen was overwhelming, so they wanted hierarchical, distinct audio. They wanted control over what is read and when the mode switches. They wanted a visual cue and connected audio to keep their place across a switch. And they wanted to review and confirm what they did by ear. Social media apps were the most common choice and had the most complex layouts, so we built Viago around them.

Study 2: evaluation

Apparatus. A Google Pixel 7 Pro running Viago and a simulated social media app, with earphones. The study ran in a coffee shop within our organization, with chairs, tables, and hanging lamps as obstacles.

Task. The app had 50 posts, 12 of them by “Judy Moore”. While walking, participants had to share her 6 posts about gardening and like her 6 other posts. Chimes at unplanned moments told them to switch modes immediately, and shares started in audio mode had to be confirmed visually. The 12 tasks took about fifteen minutes.

The Study 2 task: posts to like (top) and to share (bottom) while walking. Each dot is a chime that prompted a switch between visual mode (orange) and audio mode (blue). Figure from the paper.

Participants. Thirteen mobile users (10 male, 3 female), aged 24 to 48 (mean 35.7), who all used social media apps daily.

Measures. Success rates for the like and share tasks, 7-point Likert ratings, and video and semi-structured interviews analyzed with affinity diagramming.

What do we learn?

1. People finished the tasks while switching back and forth

Success rates were 91.67% for likes and 93.06% for shares. Participants rated their ability to understand and navigate the audio content on the go at 6.38 out of 7 (SD 0.78), and rated Viago easy to learn (5.85, SD 1.07) and easy to use (5.54, SD 1.12). As P2 put it: “It was always on the post I expected it to be on when I switched based on the feedback.” Some gestures took getting used to, for example “single tap was excessive” (P9), and “up/down and right/left were confusing when the phone is down” (P12).

Likert responses from the thirteen participants in Study 2. Figure from the paper.

2. Spatial audio and two voices helped people picture the screen

Several participants (P2, P4, P6, P9) said they pictured the layout while listening. P2: “In my mental map, I was used to the name being here (pointing left) and the actions being here (pointing right).” The different voices for text and image descriptions also worked as dividers that told people which part of a post they were in. A few still glanced at the screen, for example to check an image when its description was long.

3. Both hand-offs worked, but should take less effort

The V2A previews were rated clear (5.85, SD 1.07) and cognitively effortless (5.46, SD 1.51), and participants valued choosing which elements to bring to audio. But pressing the orange button every time felt cumbersome, and many would prefer automatic transitions. The A2V review was rated clear (5.69, SD 1.03) and cognitively effortless (6.15, SD 1.06). P4: “it had the blue boxes for me to remember where I was.” Participants often overlooked the audio headlines during review because they were focused on the screen, and they wanted a faster review, such as jumping straight to shared posts or a panel that groups liked, commented, and shared posts (P7).

4. People want this beyond social media, with caveats

Participants were willing to use Viago with other apps (6.3, SD 0.75), such as news, music, messaging, and navigation, and were open to using it on the go (5.77, SD 1.01). They also raised real-world concerns, such as ambient noise, bumping into people, and busy places that need full attention.

Design implications

  1. Automate the audio information hierarchy for different apps. Use UI semantics, existing datasets and algorithms, or large language models to group elements into audio-friendly levels, and let users adjust the result.
  2. Make transitions context-aware. Phone sensors and map services (location, activity, how busy a place is) could set how much is automated and how much information goes to audio.
  3. Personalize gestures for different apps. Interaction proxies could let users remap gestures to app functions and to levels of the audio hierarchy.
  4. Match visual and audio output to the context. For example, gaze tracking could reveal what the user has already seen so that audio fills in the rest.
  5. Extend to other devices. Smartwatches and head-mounted displays could share the work across audio, visual, and haptic output.

Limitations

The audio mode followed screen reader conventions, which may not match what sighted users expect; some participants wanted more conversational interaction with the screen. We tested only a simulated social media app, and apps with richer structure (such as Reddit) or tasks that need text input were out of scope. Study 2 was a preliminary first-use study with a small sample in a controlled setting, chosen for safety; field deployments with more people and apps are future work.

entry.title: Steering a voice assistant with a tap

link.title: Steering a voice assistant with a tap

entry.content:
Shwetha Rajaram, Hemant Bhaskar Surale, Codie McConkey, Carine Rognon, Hrim Mehta, Michael Glueck, Christopher Collins
Reality Labs Research, Meta
Conference paper · CHI '25: ACM Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems, Yokohama, Japan
PDF ACM DL Publication BibTeX
Gesture and audio-haptic techniques let users rapidly navigate and manage the timing of a conversation with a voice assistant. Here a haptic pulse on the wrist lines up with the keyword "activities" in the spoken answer, a tap on the ring selects it, and the assistant goes on to specific activities. Figure from the paper.

Quick facts

Voice assistants powered by large language models can now hold long, open-ended conversations, but speech is linear: you have to sit through long answers, interrupt out loud, and time your pauses so the assistant does not drop the conversation. We kept voice and audio for the content of the conversation and added a ring for gestures and a wristband for haptics to control its flow. The work was led by Shwetha Rajaram (University of Michigan School of Information) during a research internship at Reality Labs Research, Meta. Overall, our work contributes:

  1. A suite of multimodal interaction techniques that combine voice, gestures, audio, and haptics to facilitate conversations with voice interfaces, built into a working system.
  2. An exploratory study with 14 participants showing the benefits of these techniques for rapid access to information and flexible navigation within conversations.
  3. Design recommendations for better role-based collaboration between the input and output modalities.

Abstract

Advances in large language models (LLMs) empower new interactive capabilities for wearable voice interfaces, yet traditional voice-and-audio I/O techniques limit users’ ability to flexibly navigate information and manage timing for complex conversational tasks. We developed a suite of gesture and audio-haptic guidance techniques that enable users to control conversation flows and maintain awareness of possible future actions, while simultaneously contributing and receiving conversation content through voice and audio. A 14-participant exploratory study compared our parallelized I/O techniques to a baseline of voice-only interaction. The results demonstrate the efficiency of gestures and haptics for information access, while allowing system speech to be redirected and interrupted in a socially acceptable manner. The techniques also raised user awareness of how to leverage intelligent capabilities. Our findings inform design recommendations to facilitate role-based collaboration between multimodal I/O techniques and reduce users’ perception of time pressure when interleaving interactions with system speech.

The idea: talk for content, tap for control

Gestures and haptics carry less information than speech, but they are more efficient to perform and to process. So we gave each modality a role. Voice and audio carry the content of the conversation: your prompts and the assistant’s answers. Ring gestures steer the flow (go deeper, skip, replay, wrap up, tell me more), and wristband haptics confirm your input and point out what you can do next. Because the two pairs of channels run in parallel, you can act while the assistant is still talking.

The timeline shows one stretch of a conversation: a wrist roll wakes the mic, a haptic nudge marks a keyword while the assistant talks, Tap A cuts in to go deeper on that keyword, and a double Tap B asks for more detail without interrupting. The chart shows why each modality got its role: voice and audio are expressive but slow, while gestures and haptics are quick but less expressive.

One gesture set covers many functions because the system knows who is talking. A gesture can mean one thing while the assistant is speaking, another while you are speaking, and a third during silence.

System

Techniques. We built techniques for two kinds of flow. For navigational flow (the order of the conversation): Select a follow-up topic that the assistant reads out, Go Deeper into a keyword while the assistant is speaking, and Replay the current response or Skip to the next sentence. For temporal flow (its timing): Wake the assistant with a quick wrist rotation instead of a wake word, which also interrupts it; Restyle Response to regenerate it with new instructions; and Wrap it Up or Tell me More to end a response at the next sentence or extend it. On the output side, audio-haptic cues show when the system is listening or processing, warn with a subtle haptic after 5 seconds of silence that the conversation is about to time out (speaking within another 5 seconds keeps it going), confirm gestures, and nudge users toward keywords they can explore. Nudges are haptic only, so they do not compete with the assistant’s speech.

System architecture. The LLM-enabled voice assistant is a Unity application (A) that uses GPT-4o (E) and the Meta Voice SDK (F). Audio goes to Ray-Ban Meta glasses over Bluetooth (D), and two in-house wireless wearables handle gesture input (B) and haptic feedback (C). Figure from the paper.

Implementation. Four GPT-4o agents power the assistant: an Informational Audio Assistant that answers prompts, a Keyword Identifier that highlights important words in each answer, a Follow-up Generator that suggests subtopics, and a Response Extender that adds detail at the end of the current answer. The Meta Voice SDK (version 66.0) handles dictation, text-to-speech, and voice commands, and its word events give the timing of every spoken word, which lets nudges and gestures line up with specific words. The ring uses electrodes to sense when the index finger touches skin, plus an IMU and an optical proximity sensor, to tell apart two thumb-tap positions: A (the distal phalanx) and B (the proximal phalanx). The wristband has 4 vibrotactile actuators, and its haptic patterns match the frequency and amplitude of audio cues made with a professional sound designer. All cues were designed to be just noticeable.

Study

Conditions. Voice-Driven interaction, the baseline: speak prompts, hear answers, and use the wake word “Hey Roger” to start or interrupt. Gesture+Haptic-Guided interaction: the same voice and audio, plus gestures, a Wrist Roll to wake or interrupt, audio-haptic feedback, and haptic-only nudges on keywords.

The gesture set used in the study: three poses (Wrist Roll, Tap A, Tap B), with holds and double taps for more functions. Tap B sequences move the conversation forward, and Tap A sequences backtrack or stall it. Gestures marked (*) were introduced in Task 2. Figure from the paper.

Tasks. After a training session, participants did two tasks, each with one 2-minute conversation per condition. In Task 1 (Learning), they learned about an unfamiliar topic they chose from a list (such as “how manual clocks work” or “uses of coriander”) and then taught it back to the researchers. In Task 2 (Meeting Prep), they prepared for an upcoming meeting in a scenario of commuting to work, by asking about two meeting transcripts: one on social media strategy for a new breakfast cereal and one on a library summer reading program for kids. Task 2 added Replay, Skip, and Wrap it Up for faster-paced conversations. Condition order was counterbalanced and reversed between tasks.

Participants. 14 people (5 women, 7 men, 2 not reported), with an average age of 31 (range 21-61). 11 used voice interfaces daily. Sessions lasted 90 minutes.

Measures. Timestamped logs of user and system speech, gestures, and haptic nudges; the Subjective Assessment of Speech User Interfaces (SASSI) questionnaire after each condition; and interviews. We compared conditions with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.

What do we learn?

1. With gestures, people did more and interrupted more

Participants performed 248 interactions in the Gesture+Haptic-Guided condition versus 137 with voice alone (Z = -3.296, p = 0.001), and interrupted the assistant 58 times versus 8 (Z = -3.18, p = 0.002). Error rates did not differ significantly: 0.137 for voice input and 0.203 for gestures (Z = -1.538, p = 0.132). With voice, people let the assistant finish even when it was repeating itself, because cutting it off felt rude: “it felt like I’m talking to somebody… so I let him finish the sentence” (P4). A gesture felt different: “I don’t have to commit the act of interrupting by voice. I just kind of send a signal” (P13).

P6's two Task 1 conversations. Voice-driven turns were balanced and slower-paced, while gestures gave quicker access to information and more interruptions. Light blue bubbles are user speech, white bubbles are system speech, and blue dotted lines are interruptive gestures. Figure from the paper.

2. Gestures made information easier to reach, but the assistant felt in charge

Participants described the gesture condition as “having information at your fingertips” (P7), and the conversations had more system speech surfacing new details. The scoped gestures and nudges also showed people what the assistant could do: “knowing that the assistant can add a follow up helped me realize what all I can ask” (P2). Several participants then used the same moves by voice, saying “Tell me More” and “Replay”. On the other hand, conversations felt system-driven (“the leader in the conversation is the voice assistant,” P5), and people stuck to gestures instead of speaking: on average only 28.36% of gestures were used to wake the mic. With gestures, some participants were also unsure how the system had interpreted them, especially when selecting keywords.

3. Haptic nudges added time pressure

Combined with fast gestures, the nudges made participants feel they had to act right away or miss an opportunity. P6 described being “in a chase” with the system, and P13 felt like “multi-tasking between hearing and feeling”. On SASSI, participants rated Voice-Driven interaction significantly higher for Likeability (mean 6.016 vs 5.071; Z = 2.731, p = 0.007) and Cognitive Demand (5.329 vs 4.114, where higher is more favorable; Z = 2.605, p = 0.01), with no significant differences for System Response Accuracy, Annoyance, Habitability, or Speed. Participants attributed the higher voice ratings to their familiarity with voice interfaces and expected gestures to get easier with practice.

SASSI ratings on a 7-point scale, where higher is more favorable. Asterisks mark the two dimensions where Voice-Driven scored significantly higher. Figure from the paper.

Design implications

  1. Move between gestures and voice automatically. For example, open the mic right after a gesture so users can clarify with a few words, and use output to suggest the right input: audio prompting voice, haptics prompting gestures.
  2. Confirm how the system interpreted the input, not just that it arrived. During Go Deeper, the assistant could repeat the keyword it thinks the user picked, so mistakes are easy to correct.
  3. Give advance notice and allow delayed actions. Haptics could ramp up before a keyword arrives, and gesture variants could separate “do it now” from “queue it for later”.

Limitations

We used a ring that supports subtle on-skin gestures, and the finding that gestures are a socially acceptable way to interrupt may not hold for camera-based gesture recognition. The study ran in a controlled lab, while speech and gesture recognition would be less reliable in noisy, busy settings. Most participants were experienced voice interface users, and people with hearing or motor impairments still need to be studied. Results may include novelty effects, although participants rated the voice baseline higher on two SASSI dimensions, which suggests no bias toward the new techniques.

entry.title: One swipe decoder for many XR keyboards

link.title: One swipe decoder for many XR keyboards

entry.content:
Junxiao Shen1,2, Khadija Khaldi1, Enmin Zhou1, Hemant Bhaskar Surale1, Amy Karlson1
1Reality Labs Research, Meta  ·  2University of Bristol
Journal article · IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (presented at IEEE ISMAR 2024)
PDF IEEE Xplore Publication BibTeX
Five word-gesture keyboards: (a) mobile phone, (b) mid-air poke in AR, (c) mid-air poke in VR, (d) mid-air pinch in VR, and (e) on-surface. The bottom row shows how touch points spread around each key; every system leaves a different pattern. Figure from the paper.

Quick facts

Swipe typing (word-gesture typing) now shows up all over XR: poking a virtual keyboard, pinching to drag a ray across it, or swiping on a surface. Each mode produces differently shaped swipes, which makes a neural decoder trained on one system hard to reuse on another. Led by Junxiao Shen (Reality Labs Research, Meta and University of Bristol), we built one decoder that works across them by turning each swipe into a coarse sequence of key regions before decoding. Overall, our work contributes:

  1. Trajectory coarse discretization, which makes it possible to pre-train a word-gesture neural decoder that generalizes to on-surface and mid-air keyboards in AR and VR. The resulting Pre-trained Neural Decoder is fast, easy to deploy, and needs no extra data collection for training or fine-tuning.
  2. A validation on four AR/VR keyboard datasets (three of them collected for this work), where the Pre-trained Neural Decoder reached 90.4% Top-4 word accuracy and performed significantly better than conventional decoders.
  3. A real-time test on Quest 3: after quantization the model is 4 MB and decodes with a latency of about 97 ms.

Abstract

Text entry with word-gesture keyboards (WGK) is emerging as a popular method and becoming a key interaction for Extended Reality (XR). However, the diversity of interaction modes, keyboard sizes, and visual feedback in these environments introduces divergent word-gesture trajectory data patterns, thus leading to complexity in decoding trajectories into text. Template-matching decoding methods, such as SHARK2 [32], are commonly used for these WGK systems because they are easy to implement and configure. However, these methods are susceptible to decoding inaccuracies for noisy trajectories. While conventional neural-network-based decoders (neural decoders) trained on word-gesture trajectory data have been proposed to improve accuracy, they have their own limitations: they require extensive data for training and deep-learning expertise for implementation. To address these challenges, we propose a novel solution that combines ease of implementation with high decoding accuracy: a generalizable neural decoder enabled by pre-training on large-scale coarsely discretized word-gesture trajectories. This approach produces a ready-to-use WGK decoder that is generalizable across mid-air and on-surface WGK systems in augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR), which is evident by a robust average Top-4 accuracy of 90.4% on four diverse datasets. It significantly outperforms SHARK2 with a 37.2% enhancement and surpasses the conventional neural decoder by 7.4%. Moreover, the Pre-trained Neural Decoder’s size is only 4 MB after quantization, without sacrificing accuracy, and it can operate in real-time, executing in just 97 milliseconds on Quest 3.

The idea: snap the swipe to keys, then pre-train once

Most decoders read a swipe as a sequence of x, y coordinates. Those coordinates depend on the keyboard’s size, the input mode, and how noisy the tracking is, so a swipe on a phone and the same swipe in a headset look quite different. Instead, we assign each point of the swipe to a coarse region around a key and give the decoder a sequence of one-hot key vectors. The input then lives in the same discrete space as the output (letters), and small offsets in where the finger or cursor went stop mattering.

The keyboard view shows a swipe of "the" resampled into points (12 shown here). Each point is assigned to a key region (tinted keys), so the decoder reads a sequence of keys instead of raw coordinates; passing over y, g, f, and r is fine, because the network learns which keys were intended. The pipeline view shows the payoff: the decoder is pre-trained once on phone and synthetic swipes and then used without fine-tuning on four XR keyboards.

The decoder

Discretization. We divide the keyboard into square regions, one per key, each larger than the key itself. The region size comes from how widely touch points spread around keys in the phone dataset, and the larger “pixels” make the input more tolerant of spatial noise and ambiguity. A mapping function assigns each trajectory point to its region, and the resulting sequence is one-hot encoded.

Discretization turns a continuous swipe into a sequence of coarse "pixels" that are larger than the keys, to absorb ambiguous and noisy input. Figure from the paper.

Pre-training data. 95,649 swipes from the public “How We Swipe” phone dataset (1,338 users), plus 100,000 synthetic swipes from a GAN-based generator trained on that same phone data: 32,347 unique words in total. No XR data is used.

Model. Two stacked bidirectional LSTM layers (hidden size 222, dropout 0.3), a fully connected layer, and a CTC beam-search decoder that turns per-time-step letter probabilities into word candidates. We picked this configuration from a sweep of over 100 configurations while keeping the model under 5 MB.

Evaluation

Keyboards. Four XR keyboard systems that the decoder never saw in training: mid-air poking in AR (public HoloLens 2 data from two earlier studies, 25,513 swipes), mid-air poking and mid-air pinching in VR (Quest 2, about 51,400 swipes each), and on-surface swiping on a Sensel touchpad with the keyboard shown on a monitor (33,594 swipes).

Participants. For the VR datasets, 200 volunteers (100 women, 100 men) typed at home on a retail Quest 2, about 30 minutes per condition. For the on-surface dataset, 100 volunteers typed 160 words each in sessions of about one hour.

Baselines. SHARK2, the template-matching decoder most XR gesture keyboards use, and a conventional neural decoder with the same architecture as ours but raw Cartesian coordinates as input. We used leave-one-subject-out testing.

Measures. Top-1 and Top-4 word accuracy: how often the intended word is the first suggestion, or among the first four.

What do we learn?

1. Every XR keyboard leaves a different fingerprint

On a unit-width keyboard, touch points for AR mid-air poking sat farther from key centers (0.042 on average) than for VR poking (0.030) or VR pinching (0.028). We attribute this to less accurate hand tracking on HoloLens 2 and to the lack of hand occlusion in optical see-through AR. Phone (0.15) and on-surface (0.12) swipes were spread even more widely, a “fat finger” effect of small touch surfaces. The shapes differ too: VR swipes were straighter and more varied, and on-surface swipes were the most curved.

Curvature of swipes in the five datasets. Figure from the paper.

2. One pre-trained decoder beats both baselines out of the box

Averaged over the four XR datasets, the Pre-trained Neural Decoder reached 83.3% Top-1 and 90.4% Top-4 accuracy without any data from those keyboards. That is 37.2 percentage points above SHARK2 in Top-1 accuracy (37.6 in Top-4) and 7.4 points above the conventional neural decoder (6.9 in Top-4). Top-4 accuracy was 89.8% for AR poking, 91.9% for VR poking, 90.2% for VR pinching, and 89.5% on-surface. Adding a bigram language model and auto-correction raised the average Top-1 accuracy to 94.5%.

Decoding "quickly". (a) The raw swipe. (b) The conventional neural decoder, which reads coordinates, outputs only "quick". (c) The one-hot coarse input, which has the same shape as the output. (d) The Pre-trained Neural Decoder outputs "quickly". Red cells mark confident letters at each time step. Figure from the paper.

3. Fine-tuning helps, but only a little

Fine-tuning on each dataset’s training split raised Top-1 accuracy by 3.4 points on average (for example, from 85.1% to 88.0% for VR poking). That gain is much smaller than the gap between the pre-trained decoder and either baseline, so for research use the pre-trained decoder can be dropped in as is.

4. The encoding matters more than the region shape

One-hot encoding beat integer encoding on every dataset (83.0% vs 64.2% Top-1 on-surface, for example), likely because integers imply an order between keys that does not exist. Square and elliptical regions performed about the same, so we kept squares because they are cheaper to compute. Replacing the LSTM with a transformer kept Top-1 accuracy below 60%. After quantization, the model is 4 MB and runs with a latency of 97 ms on Quest 3, with Top-1 word accuracy unchanged.

Limitations

The decoder is built for QWERTY and may not work out of the box on other layouts such as Metropolis, OPTI, or Dvorak, because discretization assumes the QWERTY key arrangement. We validated it on four keyboard systems but did not test less common designs, such as curved keyboards or eye-gaze-based gesture typing. A transformer-based decoder performed poorly, likely because of too little training data; training one on a larger combined dataset is future work.

entry.title: Typing in mid-air with a ring

link.title: Typing in mid-air with a ring

entry.content:
Junxiao Shen1,2, Roger Boldu1, Arpit Kalla1, Michael Glueck1, Hemant Bhaskar Surale1, Amy Karlson1
1Reality Labs Research, Meta  ·  2University of Bristol
Journal article · IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (presented at IEEE ISMAR 2024)
PDF IEEE Xplore Publication BibTeX
Typing a word with RingGesture: (a) turn the wrist to place the cursor on the first letter, (b) pinch thumb and index finger to start the swipe, (c) trace the word by moving the wrist, and (d) release the pinch. Score Fusion then predicts the top words, with the first one preselected. Figure from the paper.

Quick facts

Lightweight AR glasses, built for all-day wear, can’t fit the many cameras that wide-field hand tracking needs, so text entry needs another input device. Led by Junxiao Shen (Reality Labs Research, Meta and University of Bristol), we built RingGesture: a ring that tracks the hand with an IMU and senses pinches with electrodes, so people can gesture-type in mid-air with one hand. Overall, our work contributes:

  1. RingGesture, a fast, accurate, and easy-to-learn ring-based mid-air gesture typing system, with entry rates (27.3 WPM on average, 26.4 WPM in the first block, 32.5 WPM in the last) comparable to gesture typing on a phone.
  2. Score Fusion, a lightweight deep-learning word prediction framework that combines a word-gesture decoding model (trained with a new layout transformation), a spatial spelling correction model (using a keyboard-layout-aware edit distance), and a pre-trained contextual language model.
  3. Two studies: one comparing word-level and phrase-level gesture typing (32 participants), and a longitudinal study (16 participants) showing that Score Fusion improves uncorrected character error rate by 28.2% and entry speed by 55.2% over a conventional framework, Naive Correction.

Abstract

Text entry is a critical capability for any modern computing experience, with lightweight augmented reality (AR) glasses being no exception. Designed for all-day wearability, a limitation of lightweight AR glass is the restriction to the inclusion of multiple cameras for extensive field of view in hand tracking. This constraint underscores the need for an additional input device. We propose a system to address this gap: a ring-based mid-air gesture typing technique, RingGesture, utilizing electrodes to mark the start and end of gesture trajectories and inertial measurement units (IMU) sensors for hand tracking. This method offers an intuitive experience similar to raycast-based mid-air gesture typing found in VR headsets, allowing for a seamless translation of hand movements into cursor navigation. To enhance both accuracy and input speed, we propose a novel deep-learning word prediction framework, Score Fusion, comprised of three key components: a) a word-gesture decoding model, b) a spatial spelling correction model, and c) a lightweight contextual language model. In contrast, this framework fuses the scores from the three models to predict the most likely words with higher precision. We conduct comparative and longitudinal studies to demonstrate two key findings: firstly, the overall effectiveness of RingGesture, which achieves an average text entry speed of 27.3 words per minute (WPM) and a peak performance of 47.9 WPM. Secondly, we highlight the superior performance of the Score Fusion framework, which offers a 28.2% improvement in uncorrected Character Error Rate over a conventional word prediction framework, Naive Correction, leading to a 55.2% improvement in text entry speed for RingGesture. Additionally, RingGesture received a System Usability Score of 83 signifying its excellent usability.

The idea: a ring draws the swipe, three models pick the word

Mid-air gesture typing tends to be fastest when the cursor maps directly to body movement. Vulture reached 20.6 WPM with hand control, but it relied on OptiTrack markers along the arm. RingGesture gets the same direct mapping from one ring: its IMU turns wrist rotation into cursor motion, and its electrodes detect when the thumb touches the index finger. IMU tracking adds noise and drift to the swipe, so rather than trusting the swipe alone, Score Fusion weighs it against what the keyboard layout and the conversation make likely.

The ring view shows how one word is entered: a pinch starts the swipe, wrist rotation sensed by the IMU moves the cursor, and the release ends it. The Score Fusion view shows how the word is chosen: each candidate gets three log-probability scores (from the swipe, from a keyboard-aware spelling model, and from a contextual language model), and words are ranked by their weighted sum. The baseline, Naive Correction, instead runs decoding, spelling correction, and n-gram reranking one after another.

System

Ring. We built the ring from the ElectroRing reference design (Kienzle et al.). IMU readings are converted to quaternions, then to polar coordinates, then to a 2D cursor position, with a control-display gain of 1.8. Electrodes detect the touch and release of a pinch from changes in an electrical signal.

Steady pinches. A pinch can nudge the cursor right when it matters, so the selection point lands in the wrong place (a Heisenberg effect of crosstalk between input modalities). To counter it, an exponential smoothing filter sets its own filtering level by trading off noise rejection against tracking error (λ = 0.75).

Gesture decoding model. An attention-enhanced bidirectional LSTM with CTC loss, trained on the public How We Swipe phone dataset (1,338 users, 11,318 unique words). That dataset used a different keyboard layout, so we mapped its swipes onto ours with a piecewise affine transformation anchored at key centers and six points around the keyboard. This raised the model’s test accuracy on the Study 1 data by 76% compared with simply normalizing by keyboard width and height.

Converting a swipe for "available" from the dataset's keyboard layout to ours: first resampled in time, then transformed in space using key centers and six anchor points around the keyboard. Figure from the paper.

Spatial spelling correction. A probabilistic edit distance that knows the keyboard layout. Substituting an adjacent key (like q for w) has probability 0.17, while a non-adjacent key has 0.01; omitting or adding a character each has 0.06. We estimated these from earlier mid-air gesture typing data.

Contextual language model. A bidirectional LSTM that predicts the next word from the previous words, the conversation history, and context tags such as location and time. Adding context lowered perplexity from 70.91 to 42.82, and pre-training on public comments and posts before fine-tuning lowered it to 37.16. After quantization, the model is 7 MB, small enough to run in real time on a mobile phone processor.

Experiment

Study 1: word or phrase? First, we asked whether removing the pause between words would speed up gesture typing with a directly mapped cursor. 32 participants (18 men, 13 women, 1 undisclosed; mean age 33) swiped 40 phrases per condition on a Sensel touchpad, which stands in for perfect tracking, with an idealized decoder. In the word-level condition they lifted the finger after every word; in the phrase-level condition, only after the whole phrase.

Study 2: RingGesture over two weeks. 16 participants (9 women, 6 men, 1 undisclosed; ages 21 to 49.5) wore the ring on the index finger and typed on a virtual keyboard shown on a monitor, which stands in for the fixed virtual screen of lightweight AR glasses. Over four sessions on separate days, they completed 16 blocks; each block had 10 phrases with Score Fusion and 10 with Naive Correction, in counterbalanced order. Phrases came from the ConvAI2 dataset, and each phrase’s conversation history and persona tags were fed to the language model automatically.

Study 2 setup: participants could rest their arms on the chair's armrests and move the wrist freely to swipe. Figure from the paper.

Measures. Words per minute, uncorrected and corrected character error rate, Likert ratings of six aspects (such as ease of learning and hand fatigue), and the System Usability Scale.

What do we learn?

1. Swiping word by word was as fast as swiping whole phrases, and most people preferred it

Word-level swiping reached 24.7 WPM and phrase-level 25.5 WPM, with uncorrected error rates of 7.8% and 9.2%; neither speed (F = 2.14, p = 0.13) nor accuracy differed significantly. 19 of 32 participants preferred word-level typing, citing familiarity, thinking in words, less fatigue, and immediate feedback; 8 preferred phrase-level typing and 5 had no preference. RingGesture therefore uses one swipe per word.

2. Score Fusion made ring typing 55% faster

With Score Fusion, participants averaged 27.3 WPM, against 17.6 WPM with Naive Correction (F = 30.276, p = 0.001), a 55.2% improvement. The advantage held across all 16 blocks (no condition by block interaction, p = 0.196). With Score Fusion, entry rate rose from 26.4 WPM in the first block to 32.5 WPM in the last, and peak performance reached 47.9 WPM.

Entry rate over 16 blocks with Score Fusion and Naive Correction, with fitted power-law learning curves. Figure from the paper.

3. Every model in the fusion pulls its weight

Score Fusion also lowered the uncorrected character error rate by 28.2% and the corrected one by 29.0% relative to Naive Correction. Replaying the swipes logged in Study 2, the gesture decoding model alone had a character error rate of 27.86%; adding spatial spelling correction brought it to 12.12%, and adding the contextual language model brought it to 5.56%.

(a) Uncorrected and (b) corrected character error rate under the two conditions. Figure from the paper.

4. People found it easy to use

RingGesture scored 83 on the System Usability Scale, where anything above 80 indicates excellent usability. Participants found it easy to learn, reported little hand fatigue, and were neutral about eye fatigue. Learning curves suggest they started faster with Score Fusion (fitted initial rate 23.9 vs 14.1 WPM) but improved faster with Naive Correction (learning rate 0.115 vs 0.069), possibly because they had to adapt to its weaker predictions. Two participants occasionally triggered a false pinch when the middle finger touched the index finger.

Limitations

We used a monitor as a stand-in for lightweight AR glasses, which show a virtual screen at a fixed distance with only 3DOF. That holds in a controlled lab but may not extend to real-world use, especially on the move; testing in the wild (typing while walking, in a car, or lying in bed) waits for glasses with longer battery life. The conversational context was predefined with each phrase rather than coming from participants’ own conversations. We have not yet tested Score Fusion with other text entry methods, such as touch typing.

entry.title: Smartphone typing without the smartphone
entry.content:
Taejun Kim1,3, Amy Karlson1, Aakar Gupta1, Tovi Grossman2, Jason Wu1,4, Parastoo Abtahi1, Christopher Collins1, Michael Glueck1, Hemant Bhaskar Surale1
1Reality Labs Research, Meta  ·  2University of Toronto  ·  3KAIST  ·  4Carnegie Mellon University
Conference paper · UIST '23: ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology, San Francisco, CA, USA
PDF ACM DL Publication BibTeX
(a) Two-thumb typing on a physical smartphone. (b) STAR: the same two-thumb typing on a virtual keyboard overlaid on your hands in AR. Figure from the paper.

Quick facts

Led by Taejun Kim as a research intern at Reality Labs Research, Meta. STAR lets you type in AR the way you type on a phone: hold your hands as if gripping one, and tap with both thumbs on a virtual keyboard overlaid on the sides of your index fingers. Overall, our work contributes:

  1. STAR, an on-skin, smartphone-analogous AR text entry technique that reuses the two-thumb typing skills people already have from their phones.
  2. An exploration of skill transfer from smartphone typing to AR. An elicitation study with 29 participants found three hand postures for typing on an imaginary phone, and we then tested these postures and other design parameters to keep the skill transferable.
  3. An analysis of the gap between STAR and smartphone typing, which shows that better hand tracking and thumb tap sensing could bring STAR closer to phone typing speeds.

Abstract

While text entry is an essential and frequent task in Augmented Reality (AR) applications, devising an efficient and easy-to-use text entry method for AR remains an open challenge. This research presents STAR, a smartphone-analogous AR text entry technique that leverages a user’s familiarity with smartphone two-thumb typing. With STAR, a user performs thumb typing on a virtual QWERTY keyboard that is overlain on the skin of their hands. During an evaluation study of STAR, participants achieved a mean typing speed of 21.9 WPM (i.e., 56% of their smartphone typing speed), and a mean error rate of 0.3% after 30 minutes of practice. We further analyze the major factors implicated in the performance gap between STAR and smartphone typing, and discuss ways this gap could be narrowed.

The idea: keep the skill, drop the phone

Two-thumb typing on a phone is a fast skill most people already have. Bare-hand text entry in AR usually asks for something new instead (mid-air typing, eye typing, tapping on a fingertip), and mid-air keyboards give you nothing to press against. STAR keeps what transfers from the phone: the grip, the QWERTY layout, the thumb movements, and a physical surface under the thumbs. Your own skin takes the place of the touchscreen.

One tap, seen from the side. The headset tracks all three thumb joints, and the projection arc shows where the curving thumb will land, which is not always the key straight below the tip. Capacitive tape on the thumb tip detects the touch, and the key with the closest center registers. The front view shows the Enlarged keyboard with its two word suggestions.

How a typing session works:

  • Open and close. Making the “knuckle posture” opens the keyboard over your hands, and releasing it closes the keyboard. The hand contact makes the mode switch explicit and prevents false activations.
  • See your thumbs. STAR draws all three tracked thumb joints and a projection arc from the thumb tip to the keyboard, and highlights the key at the end of the arc. With only the thumb tip shown, people often hit the key next to the one they aimed at, because the thumb tip moves in an arc rather than straight down.
  • Feel the tap. Each tap lands on your own skin, so there is real haptic feedback.
  • Finish words. A decoder combines where each tap landed (a bivariate Gaussian around each key) with word frequencies and offers the two most likely words above the keyboard.

Designing STAR

Elicitation. Over video calls, 29 people (19 women, 10 men, mean age 38) typed “The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog” on an imaginary phone in their hands. 27 of them used both thumbs, and 26 of those 27 kept their hands in contact. Three postures emerged: the Nested Finger Surface (n = 20), the Index Finger Surface (n = 6), and the Single Palm Surface (n = 2).

Typing surface. In a HoloLens 2 prototype, the Nested Finger Surface was uneven, because one hand sits behind the other, and taps were unstable. The flatter Index Finger Surface gave more consistent presses, so we chose it even though fewer participants had proposed it.

Positioning. A keyboard that followed the hands still shook with tracking jitter, even with a 1-euro filter, and with gaps of 1–2 mm between keys even a tiny shift caused errors. A Stationary keyboard, fixed where the knuckle posture was made, let people type more confidently.

Size. The phone’s own layout (5.5 mm keys, 1 mm apart) was too small for about ±1 mm of tracking jitter. After trying 6, 7, and 8 mm keys with 2, 3, and 4 mm gaps, we chose an Enlarged keyboard with 6 mm keys and 2 mm gaps.

The three design parameters we explored: (a) typing surface, (b) keyboard positioning, and (c) keyboard size. The bold options (Index Finger Surface, Stationary, Enlarged) became STAR. Figure from the paper.

System

STAR runs as a Unity app on a Microsoft HoloLens 2 (52° diagonal field of view). Its hand tracking had a latency of about 90 ms and a jitter of about ±1 mm, which shaped choices such as the Stationary keyboard. Tracking alone could not tell exactly when a thumb touched the finger, so key presses and the felt touch were often out of sync. For the study, we put capacitive tape on each thumb tip, read by an Arduino and relayed through a PC to the headset over TCP: a tap started when the reading rose above 250 and ended when it fell below 200.

Using STAR: (a) make the knuckle posture, (b) type with both thumbs on the sides of the index fingers, and (c) release the posture to leave typing mode. (d) The visualized thumb tip and projection arc. Figure from the paper.

Experiment

Conditions. STAR, plus typing on a physical smartphone as a baseline. The goal was to see how close STAR could get to the phone, not to beat it, so the smartphone was tested once before and once after the STAR blocks. The two smartphone speeds did not differ significantly (39.9 vs. 39.0 WPM), so we averaged them into a 39.4 WPM baseline.

Apparatus. STAR on the HoloLens 2 with the thumb-tip capacitive tape, as described above. The smartphone baseline was a Galaxy A13 5G running an Android app with the Original keyboard layout.

Task. Participants sat on a chair without armrests, facing a plain wall, and transcribed phrases from the MacKenzie and Soukoreff phrase set. Each block had ten phrases: one smartphone block, five STAR blocks, then a final smartphone block, with breaks of at least two minutes. The whole session took about two hours.

Participants. Ten people from a university community (2 women, 8 men, mean age 25). Eight had no prior AR experience, two were left-handed, and two wore glasses.

Measures. Text entry speed in words per minute (WPM), uncorrected error rate (UER), corrected error rate (CER, which also counts backspaced errors), backspace count, inter-key interval (IKI), and key press duration (KPD), plus a post-study interview.

What do we learn?

1. About 22 WPM after 30 minutes

Typing speed rose from 17.4 WPM in Block 1 to 21.9 WPM in Block 5 (F(4,36) = 10.996, p < .001). That is 56% of participants’ smartphone speed of 39.4 WPM. In the last block, the fastest participant reached 25.0 WPM and the slowest 16.4 WPM.

Text entry speed, inter-key interval, and key press duration across the five STAR blocks, with the smartphone baseline as a dashed line. Error bars show standard deviation. Figure from the paper.

2. Errors stayed at smartphone levels

Uncorrected errors averaged 0.2% with STAR and 0.5% with the smartphone (0.3% in STAR’s last block). Corrected error rates (8.5% vs. 8.3%) and backspace use (3 vs. 2.6) were also similar, so people fixed mistakes about as often as on a phone. None of the error measures changed significantly across STAR blocks.

3. The gap is in the timing, and hand tracking is the main cause

In Block 5, the time between keys was 585 ms with STAR versus 315 ms on the phone, 1.9 times longer, which matches the speed ratio. Each press also lasted longer (139 ms vs. 84 ms). Half of the participants said they had to keep checking the visualized thumb to avoid mistakes. P6 put it this way: “the [visualized] thumb couldn’t follow my speed when I moved my finger quickly from one key to another”. We suspect people waited for the lagging thumb marker to confirm that the right key had been pressed.

HoloLens 2 thumb tracking: (a) the tracked position lags the measured position during a roughly 200 mm movement, and (b) it jitters while the hand is held still. Figure from the paper.

The fixed keyboard also played a role. On a phone, the keys move with your hands, so muscle memory works. With the Stationary keyboard, people had to keep their hands aligned with it, and three participants asked for a keyboard that follows the hands: the design we had dropped because tracking was too unstable. We expect STAR to get closer to phone speeds as headset tracking improves, or with extra sensing that leaves the thumbs free, such as rings, smartwatches, or bracelets.

Limitations

STAR was not fully bare-hand in our study: capacitive tape on the thumb tips sensed the taps. A real deployment needs robust hand tracking and tap sensing, which is hard from the headset alone because parts of the hand can be hidden from its cameras. We tested only in a lab, seated, in front of a plain wall, so typing while standing, walking, lying down, or doing something else is untested. Because we used the headset’s own tracking rather than motion capture, STAR’s performance with ideal tracking is still unknown; varying latency and jitter systematically could show how much precision smartphone-level typing needs. We studied two-thumb typing with one standard keyboard size, so one-handed STAR (for example, with gesture typing) and keyboards sized to each person’s hands remain open.
