entry.title: Switch menu modes with a glance

link.title: Switch menu modes with a glance

entry.content:
Yanfei Hu Fleischhauer1, Hemant Surale2, Florian Alt3, Ken Pfeuffer3,4
1LMU Munich  ·  2University of Waterloo  ·  3Bundeswehr University Munich  ·  4Aarhus University
Short paper · ETRA '23: 2023 Symposium on Eye Tracking Research and Applications, Tübingen, Germany
PDF ACM DL Publication BibTeX
The setup: a Microsoft Surface Pro 4 tilted at 60°, with a Tobii 4c eye tracker below the screen. The participant crosses arrow targets with the pen and switches modes with the menu at the top. Figure from the paper.

Quick facts

Changing modes on a tablet usually means moving the pen or finger up to a menu and back. We let the eyes make that trip instead: look at the menu item, then confirm by dwelling or with a tap wherever the hand already is. Led by Yanfei Hu Fleischhauer (LMU Munich). Overall, our work contributes:

  1. The first investigation of mode-switching between manual and gaze input, using the subtraction method to isolate the cost of a mode switch inside a drawing workflow.
  2. Empirical evidence (N=18) that users switch efficiently between gaze and hand, that gaze saves manual effort, and that users prefer gaze-based methods over the familiar hand baseline.
  3. A new technique, GazeTap*, that unifies selecting a mode and applying it, and saved substantial time in a follow-up study (N=6).

Abstract

In design work, a common task is the interaction with menus to change the drawing mode. Done frequently, this can become a tedious and fatiguing task, especially for tablets where users physically employ a stylus or finger touch. As our eyes are naturally involved in visual search and acquisition of desired menu items, we propose gaze to shortcut the physical movement. We investigate gaze-based mode-switching for menus in tablets by a novel mode-switching methodology, assessing a gaze-only (dwell-time) and multimodal (gaze and tap) technique, compared to hand-based interaction. The results suggest that users can efficiently alternate between manual and eye input when interacting with the menu; both gaze-based techniques have lower physical demand and individual speed-error trade-offs. This led to a novel technique that substantially reduces time by unifying mode-selection and mode-application. Our work points to new roles for our eyes to efficiently short-cut menu actions during the workflow.

The idea: let the eyes make the trip to the menu

A mode switch has three steps: find the menu item, move the hand to select it, and move the hand back to the workspace. The eyes already do the first step, so we let them do the selection as well, and the hand stays on the canvas. To measure what one switch costs inside a real workflow, rather than in an isolated selection task, we used the subtraction method.

Four ways to switch to the next mode before crossing the outlined target. With the hand baseline, the pen travels to the menu and back. With Dwell, resting the eyes on the item for 0.5 s selects it. With GazeTap, the user looks at the item and taps wherever the pen already is. GazeTap* (follow-up study) turns that touch into the start of the next stroke. The second panel shows how the subtraction method isolates the time of one mode switch.

Experiment

Techniques. Dwell: looking at a menu item for 500 ms selects it, with visual feedback when the item is viewed and when the selection is confirmed. GazeTap: look at the item (its border highlights), then tap with the pen or finger at the current position to confirm. Baseline: move the pen or finger to the menu item, the default in today’s apps. Each technique was done with the pen and with finger touch, giving 3 × 2 conditions in Latin square order.

GazeTap: pen input on the canvas (1), gaze hovers on a menu item (2), and a tap with the pen confirms the switch (3). Figure from the paper.

Task. Participants crossed rectangles with strokes, a task adapted from Dillon et al. and Surale et al. Baseline blocks had five crossings and no menu selection. Compound blocks had the same five crossings, but before crossings 2 and 4 the participant had to select the color mode that matched the outlined target. Menu items appeared at three positions along the top of the screen, and the crossing direction changed between blocks, for 720 crossings per participant.

The start of a compound block with the pen baseline: cross the first target, switch mode at the menu, then cross the second and third targets. Crossings 4 and 5 repeat the pattern. Figure from the paper.

Apparatus. Software written in Java with Processing on a Microsoft Surface Pro 4 (12.3”, 2736×1824 px) with a Surface Pen and a Tobii 4c eye tracker, with participants seated about 60 cm from the screen. Gaze techniques used an invisible 4×4 cm selection area around each menu item, and a post-hoc check put gaze accuracy at about 1 cm (about 0.954° of visual angle). The crossing targets sat on the right side of the screen so that the hands would not block the eye tracker.

Participants. 18 paid participants (9 female, 9 male, all right-handed), aged 20 to 56 (M = 27.97). On a 1 to 5 scale they rated themselves as moderately experienced with tablets (M = 3.77) and less experienced with gaze (M = 2.37) and pen input (M = 1.9). A session took 45 to 50 minutes.

Measures. Menu selection time from the subtraction method (mean cycle time in compound blocks minus mean cycle time in baseline blocks); crossing, out-of-target, and mode errors; six usability ratings; and a final ranking of the techniques.

What do we learn?

1. People mix eyes and hands without trouble

All participants used gaze for quick menu switches during hand-controlled drawing, in every trial, after about 30 seconds of training per technique. Both gaze techniques removed the hand’s trip to the menu, and hand fatigue was rated significantly lower for Dwell and GazeTap than for the manual baseline. The trade-off was eye fatigue, which was rated higher for Dwell than for the baseline.

2. Skipping the hand trip cost about a quarter of a second

Mean menu selection time was 1003 ms for the manual baseline, 1236 ms for Dwell, and 1246 ms for GazeTap. The baseline was significantly faster than both gaze techniques (F(1.715, 29.161) = 12.032, p < .001). Between the two gaze techniques, Dwell caused significantly fewer errors than GazeTap and was rated easier to use and faster.

Menu selection time by technique, device (pen or touch), and menu position, with 95% confidence intervals. Figure from the paper.

3. Most people still preferred gaze

16 of 18 participants ranked a gaze technique first: Dwell 9 times (5 with pen, 4 with touch) and GazeTap 7 times (5 with pen, 2 with touch), against 2 for the hand baseline. P16: “Gaze dwell is very intuitive, as you automatically look at the colour square”. Those who preferred the hand found the coordination hard: “I thought it is difficult to switch between two modalities” (P9).

4. Keep drawing after the tap, and switching gets much faster

GazeTap* extends GazeTap: the user looks at the menu item and touches down to switch the mode, then keeps dragging to draw the line without lifting the pen or finger. This joins selecting a mode and applying it into one continuous action. In a follow-up with 6 participants, menu selection time with GazeTap* averaged about 519 ms (525 ms pen, 513 ms touch), 46.6% faster than the manual baseline and 59.8% faster than Dwell (both p < .001).

Follow-up study (N=6) with GazeTap*: menu selection time (a), combined error rate (b), and error types (c). Figure from the paper.

Errors went up (6.94% with pen and 10.28% with touch, versus about 4% for the others), although post-hoc tests found no significant differences. Gaze data suggests why: with GazeTap*, the eyes were still far from the target, on the menu, when the stroke began, so users started drawing eyes-free. The technique may therefore suit rapid, short ink strokes, or tasks where the stroke does not need to start at a precise spot.

Limitations

We ran both studies in a lab. On the move, hands may be less steady, which could make gaze shortcuts more useful, but eye tracking may be less precise. Participants were students and employees of the local university; other groups, such as older users, may benefit more from reduced physical effort. The follow-up study was small (N=6) and has limited statistical power. Finally, our menu targets were large by the standards of regular menus, though typical for gaze interfaces; nested menus could address this.

entry.title: Dropping in on a friend’s smartglasses

link.title: Dropping in on a friend’s smartglasses

entry.content:
Hemant Bhaskar Surale1,2, Yu Jiang Tham2, Brian A. Smith2,3,*, Rajan Vaish2,*
1University of Waterloo, Canada  ·  2Snap Inc., USA  ·  3Columbia University, USA  ·  *Co-principal investigators
Conference paper · AHs '22: Augmented Humans 2022, Kashiwa, Chiba, Japan
PDF (preprint) ACM DL arXiv Publication BibTeX
ARcall's three components. Drop-In: (a) the Friend sees the Wearer's view on a smartphone. ARaction: (b) the Friend picks an AR rainbow, and (c) the Wearer sees it augmenting their reality. Micro-Chat: (d) the Friend laughs after sending it, and (e) the Wearer reacts, while the Friend stays dropped in. Figure from the paper.

Quick facts

Today, sharing AR with a friend often means sending a pre-recorded video with effects on top, without knowing where they are. ARcall instead connects a friend on a smartphone with a smartglasses wearer in real time: the friend sees the wearer’s view, places AR content directly into it, and the two talk, in short sessions that respect the glasses’ battery and the wearer’s privacy. Overall, our work contributes:

  1. An understanding of user behaviour and affordances created by this AR-based, real-time communication method, with a design that takes into account the practical limits of modern smartglasses.
  2. A qualitative evaluation of ARcall’s key components with 14 participants, showing the importance of context priming through Drop-In, engagement through ARaction, and meaningful conversation through Micro-Chat.

Abstract

Augmented Reality (AR) smartglasses are increasingly regarded as the next generation personal computing platform. However, there is a lack of understanding about how to design communication systems using them. We present ARcall, a novel Augmented Reality-based real-time communication system that enables an immersive, delightful, and privacy-preserving experience between a smartphone user and a smartglasses wearer. ARcall allows a remote friend (Friend) to send and project AR content to a smartglasses wearer (Wearer). The ARcall system was designed with the practical limits of existing AR glasses in mind, including shorter battery life and a reduced field of view. We conduct a qualitative evaluation of the three main components of ARcall: Drop-In, ARaction, and Micro-Chat. Our results provide novel insights for building future AR-based communication methods, including, the importance of context priming, user control over AR content placement, and the feeling of co-presence while conversing.

The idea: drop in, augment, talk

The Wearer starts an ARcall session and invites one Friend. During that session the Friend can drop in at any time, see what the Wearer sees, send AR content into the Wearer’s glasses, and talk. Each drop-in is short to save the glasses’ battery, and only the Wearer can extend it.

What flows between the two devices, and what each person controls. Time runs downward in the session view: an ARcall session holds any number of short drop-ins, and the Wearer can extend a drop-in in 30-second steps.

Each component answers a practical problem with AR glasses. Drop-In lets the Friend check the Wearer’s context before doing anything, the way a caller might ask “is this a good time?”. ARaction augments the Wearer’s world directly, instead of sending pre-recorded AR content or streaming the caller. Micro-Chat keeps voice short, because streaming video and audio drains smartglasses batteries quickly.

System

Design considerations. We designed ARcall around five considerations: give the Wearer control and the Friend freedom (D1), respect the Wearer’s privacy (D2), make AR content relevant and well placed (D3), accommodate the narrow field of view (D4), and handle power constraints (D5). For example, invitations are for a single Friend and expire automatically, the Wearer can blur their video feed, and AR content is restricted to virtual objects rather than whole-world reskins, since Wearers found partial augmentation more compelling.

ARcall's architecture: (a) the Friend App to drop in, send AR content, and talk; (b) a web server for video streaming, friendships, and call settings; (c) the Wearer App to configure and start sessions, and the Glass App that displays the AR content. Figure from the paper.

Drop-In. In the Wearer App, the Wearer picks the Friend, a blur level from 0 (clear video) to 10 (fully blurred), the ARcall session length (5 minutes to an hour), and the Drop-In length. We tested how long the glasses could stream video before getting too hot, and limited each drop-in to between 30 seconds and one minute. The Friend gets an invitation and can drop in at any time by tapping it, which shows the Wearer’s camera feed in the center of the phone.

ARaction. The Friend scrolls through a carousel of ten pieces of AR content and sends one with a tap. Animated 3D objects, such as a bird or a dragon, appear in the middle of the glasses’ display and follow the Wearer’s head. Particle effects, such as snow, cover the whole display. One piece is shown at a time, but the Friend can send as many as they like.

The Friend selects an AR phoenix from the carousel in the Friend App, and it is immediately projected into the Wearer's view. Figure from the paper.

Micro-Chat. A voice call starts as soon as the Friend drops in and lasts as long as the drop-in. The Glass App shows a countdown, and the Wearer can add 30 seconds at a time by pressing a button on the right temple of the glasses. The Friend can mute or unmute their microphone.

Implementation. We built ARcall on Snap’s 4th generation AR Spectacles (2021). The Glass App is written in Java for Android, and the Wearer and Friend Apps in Swift for iOS (the Friend App renders AR with ARKit, SceneKit, and SpriteKit). Video calls use the Sinch API, settings are stored in Firebase, and end-to-end latency is around 100 ms.

First-use study

Participants. 14 people (4 women, 10 men; 2 in their 20s and 12 in their 30s) took part in pairs of friends, for seven sessions in total. Six had used smartglasses before.

Procedure. After a 20-minute onboarding, the Wearer took a walk outside and invited the Friend, who stayed in a conference room, and the pair used ARcall for 10 to 15 minutes. Since the study ran during the holiday season, the AR content was holiday and fantasy themed. To see whether context shaped what Friends sent, we placed six visual artifacts along the Wearer’s path, each subtly matching a piece of AR content (for example, a news poster with a dragon). Each session took about an hour.

Measures. App logs, a post-experience questionnaire with 7-point Likert items (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree), and a semi-structured interview. Two researchers coded the responses and merged their findings into themes.

What do we learn?

1. People kept dropping in and extending

The median drop-in lasted 1.9 minutes, and Friends sent a median of 11 pieces of AR content per drop-in. Over 200 pieces were sent in total, and Wearers extended drop-ins 48 times. Overall, participants felt ARcall would add great value to smartglasses (median 6 of 7).

2. Seeing the Wearer’s view made AR content feel personal

Wearers felt the content their Friends sent was relevant to their context (median 6), that it augmented their reality (median 6), and that they understood the intent behind it (median 6). Friends picked up on the artifacts we had placed on the path, so Wearers felt the content was hand-picked: “Based on what I was looking at, they augmented the AR content to my reality, and it was pretty spot on” (W3). Both sides also described the content as surprising and fun.

Visual artifacts we placed along the Wearer's path (top) and the AR content they matched (bottom): (a) holiday ornaments; (b) a dragon. Figure from the paper.

3. Invite-only felt safe, but Wearers wanted to know when a Friend arrived

Wearers strongly agreed that the invite-only design was important for controlling their privacy (median 7). Most set drop-ins to the maximum of one minute and chose “No Blur”; one Wearer started with full blur and switched to no blur once they began using ARcall. Friends did not feel they were invading the Wearer’s privacy (median 6). But ARcall gave no signal when a Friend dropped in, which we did on purpose to keep the AR a surprise, and some Wearers wanted one: “unless my friend [projected] an AR experience, I couldn’t tell if they had joined” (W7).

4. Voice turned AR into a shared moment

Wearers felt together with their Friend as soon as they heard them talk (median 6), and Friends found it important to get the Wearer’s reaction to the content they sent (median 6). “I think more than the AR experience, the voice chat was fantastic” (W3). A few Friends found the time limit short, although the Wearer could always extend it.

Design implications

  1. Let Wearers know when a Friend drops in, for example with a “John just dropped-in!” message, a snooze option, or an LED-like notification instead of the content itself.
  2. Offer a wide variety of AR content and scene-based recommendations, such as suggesting a beach ball or a sandcastle when the Wearer is at the beach, while balancing automation with freedom of expression.
  3. Minimize the difference between how the Friend and the Wearer see content. Snow filled the Friend’s phone screen edge to edge, but not the Wearer’s field of view, which made the display edge obvious and broke immersion.
  4. Make AR content movable and anchor it to real-world objects and surfaces. Content that took over the view sometimes occluded what the Wearer was doing, such as reading.
  5. Treat short Micro-Chats as a social feature, not only a battery saver. Brief drop-ins can work like a hallway chat or office hours.

Limitations

ARcall is a proof of concept evaluated in a first-use study with 14 participants who came as pairs of friends. Their trust in each other may be why most did not use the blur setting, which may matter more in other contexts or relationships. The AR content was limited to ten themed items that were positioned automatically and could not be moved. We also did not investigate other ways to save power, such as lowering display brightness or using only one side of the display, or sessions with more than one Friend.

entry.title: Keyboard shortcuts without pressing a key

link.title: Keyboard shortcuts without pressing a key

entry.content:
Nalin Chhibber1, Hemant Surale1, Fabrice Matulic2, Daniel Vogel1
1School of Computer Science, University of Waterloo  ·  2Preferred Networks Inc.
Journal article · Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction, Vol. 5, ISS, Article 486 (presented at ACM ISS 2021)
🏆 Best Paper Honorable Mention Award
PDF ACM DL Project page Code Dataset Publication BibTeX
Different postures trigger different commands: (a) an open left hand at 90° wrist rotation beside the keyboard decreases the volume; (b) an open left hand at 0° on the keyboard opens a snipping tool; (c) a closed right hand at 0° below the keyboard turns the car in a racing game; (d) an open right hand at 0° on the keyboard advances a page; (e) an open right hand at 90° beside the keyboard increases the volume. Figure from the paper.

Quick facts

Keyboard shortcuts mean finding and pressing the right keys. Typealike recognizes simple hand postures made on, beside, or below a laptop keyboard, with no key press, using only the built-in webcam and a mirror reflector. The work was led by Nalin Chhibber (University of Waterloo). Overall, our work contributes:

  1. A set of near-keyboard hand postures that are acceptable to users, recognized reliably (97.4% accuracy across 36 postures and two non-posture classes), and fast to perform (1139 ms on average, versus 1738 ms for keyboard shortcuts).
  2. A dataset of nearly 350K posture images captured under different lighting conditions and two keyboard backgrounds, released with our code, experiment trial data, and trained model.

Abstract

We propose a style of hand postures to trigger commands on a laptop. The key idea is to perform hand-postures while keeping the hands on, beside, or below the keyboard, to align with natural laptop usage. 36 hand-posture variations are explored considering three resting locations, left or right hand, open or closed hand, and three wrist rotation angles. A 30-participant formative study measures posture preferences and generates a dataset of nearly 350K images under different lighting conditions and backgrounds. A deep learning recognizer achieves over 97% accuracy when classifying all 36 postures with 2 additional non-posture classes for typing and non-typing. A second experiment with 20 participants validates the recognizer under real-time usage and compares posture invocation time with keyboard shortcuts. Results find low error rates and fast formation time, indicating postures are close to current typing and pointing postures. Finally, practical use case demonstrations are presented, and further extensions discussed.

The idea: the posture is the shortcut

Earlier techniques recognize a hand posture at the moment a key is pressed, so the key press marks when to look. But touch typing already pairs each key press with automatic hand movements, and some postures are awkward to hold while pressing a key. Typealike drops the key press. A mirror reflector turns the built-in webcam down toward the keyboard, and a classifier labels every frame. So that ordinary typing is not mistaken for a command, the classifier also learns two non-posture classes: typing, and non-typing (clicking, resting, or no hands in view).

How Typealike reads a posture: the mirror points the webcam at the keyboard, and each frame is classified as one of 36 postures or as typing or non-typing. A posture is one choice from each of four parameters; the highlighted choice is the volume-down posture from the first figure.

The posture set follows three design considerations from the paper:

  • Recognition without a key press, so commands do not conflict with touch-typing motor behavior. Every posture uses a slightly extended thumb to look distinct from typing, touchpad use, and resting.
  • Performed on or near the keyboard, with the wrist staying in contact with the laptop case. This keeps the move from typing to a command short, similar to the goal of minimizing homing time for pointing.
  • Simple and easy to perform, so they are comfortable enough to be practical. Postures can be formed in a relaxed way, without forcibly clenching a fist or rigidly extending the thumb.

The posture set

Posture parameters: (a) the surface where the posture is performed (on, below, or beside the keyboard); (b, c) closed or open hand form at 0°, 90°, or 180° wrist orientation. All postures use an extended thumb and can be performed with either hand. Figure from the paper.

Each of the 36 postures is defined by four parameters:

  • Hand: dominant or non-dominant.
  • Form: a predominantly open or closed hand, thumb extended in both.
  • Orientation: the palm touching the surface (0°), the side edge of the hand (90°), or the back of the hand (180°).
  • Surface: on the central keyboard area, beside the keyboard (left or right, depending on the hand), or just below it. These are places where hands already rest while typing, resting, or using the touchpad.

Experiment 1: preferences and a dataset

Participants. 30 people (10 female, 20 male), aged 19 to 31 (mean 24.6), 23 of them right-handed, with a mean typing speed of 38 words per minute.

Apparatus. A 2018 15-inch MacBook Pro. The built-in camera, fitted with a mirror reflector, recorded the hands at 30 FPS in 1280×720. Twenty participants used a green keyboard and laptop cover, so the background could later be replaced through chromakeying. Lighting changed per block: diffuse ambient light in one block and a light source on the left or right side in the others.

Apparatus: (a) mirror reflector on the built-in camera; (b) approximate hand capture volume; (c) camera view; (d) camera view with the green keyboard cover. Figure from the paper.

Task. Short game-like trials, each up to 6 seconds: typing a five-letter word, pressing a shortcut (Shift, Ctrl, or Alt plus a letter), clicking a button with the touchpad, or holding a prompted posture. The posture prompt wiggled slightly, and participants mimicked it, which added variety to the images.

Design. Three blocks of 36 posture trials, each followed by a typing or clicking reference task: 216 trials per participant, about 25 minutes. At the end, participants rated every posture for comfort and overall preference on a 5-point scale.

Recognizer. We extracted frames from the last 2 seconds of each posture trial, plus typing and non-typing frames, for nearly 350K labeled images. A ResNet-50 network pre-trained on ImageNet was fine-tuned on 38 classes. For augmentation, we replaced the green background with random images and varied brightness by up to 20%. We tested with 10 random splits of 24 training and 6 validation participants, so the model was always evaluated on people it had never seen.

Experiment 2: postures versus shortcuts in real time

Participants. 20 new people (8 female, 12 male), aged 23 to 33 (mean 27.25), 14 right-handed and 6 left-handed, with a mean typing speed of 46 words per minute.

Apparatus. The same laptop and mirror, without the green cover and under normal room lighting. The recognizer ran at 30 FPS on the same laptop.

Task. The same tasks, but a posture trial ended as soon as the correct posture was recognized. Keyboard shortcuts served as a relative baseline.

Design. Five blocks, each with a sequence of 36 posture trials and a sequence of 36 shortcut trials, alternating with typing or clicking trials: 720 trials per participant. The first block was slower for postures, so we analyzed the last four.

Measures. Task completion time; Transition-In time, from the prompt to the first correct input; Transition-Out time, from the last input to the next prompt; and errors.

What do we learn?

1. Postures can be recognized without a key press

Across the 10 participant splits, the recognizer reached 97.4% accuracy (error rate 2.6%, sd 0.9%). Most confusions involved the typing and non-typing classes, and some automatically labeled frames turned out to be wrong, so a manual review of the labels could raise accuracy further. In real-time use, posture trial errors (no correct posture within 6 s) happened 6 times, and mode errors (the wrong posture) occurred in 4% of posture trials, compared with 3% for shortcuts.

2. Postures are faster to start, shortcuts are faster to leave

Postures took 1139 ms on average, versus 1738 ms for shortcuts. Postures had a 600 ms faster Transition-In time, but a 490 ms slower Transition-Out time. The gap was largest when returning to typing: 105 ms after a shortcut versus 1148 ms after a posture, which is no surprise since shortcuts are very close to typing.

Transition-In time (top) and Transition-Out time (bottom) for shortcuts and postures, coming from or going to a typing or clicking task. Figure from the paper.

This comparison checks that postures fit alongside existing keyboard operations. It does not present postures as a replacement for shortcuts, which have a larger vocabulary and stay close to typing.

3. The 180° wrist turn is the least comfortable

Postures with a 180° wrist rotation were rated lowest for comfort (2.2, versus 3.7 for 90° and 3.8 for 0°) and for preference (2.3, versus 3.5 and 3.6). Postures below the keyboard were preferred over those beside it (3.4 versus 2.9). The most comfortable posture was the dominant open hand at 0° on the keyboard (4.36). The 90° postures were also the fastest to perform (1056.5 ms, versus 1189.5 ms at 0° and 1179 ms at 180°).

Mean comfort and overall preference ratings by (a) orientation, (b) form, (c) hand, and (d) surface. Error bars are 95% CI. Figure from the paper.

Design implications

  1. Avoid postures without wrist rotation during text entry. The 0° postures are closest to typing, so they can interfere with typing and confuse the recognizer.
  2. Save the 180° rotation for explicit, infrequent commands, such as locking the screen or closing all applications.
  3. Use local surfaces for in-situ commands. For example, select text with the touchpad, form a posture to copy, select a destination, and form a posture to paste, all without a key press.
  4. Use the non-dominant hand for quick commands. Non-dominant postures were slightly faster, so they could serve as a general mode switch.

We demonstrated postures for system volume, page turning, switching to the eraser in a drawing application, opening a snipping tool, and controlling a racing game. We also tried two-handed postures, such as locking the screen with both hands closed at 180°.

Limitations

Our tasks balanced typing, clicking, shortcuts, and postures equally, while real tasks may mix them in different proportions. Shortcuts were prompted at random from a limited set, which may have added mental overhead, since real shortcut use benefits from repetition and motor memory. All sessions took place in a static indoor setting on the same device, and participants avoided tilting the screen in the first experiment. A real system would need more context to reject unintended postures. A real deployment could also replace the mirror with an ultra wide-angle lens, a pop-out mirror, or a rotating camera.
